segments: 235. And many ferrymen whom they found, they drowned in the Tigris.
And many people fled from their houses
and took refuge in the neighborhood of the Caliph's palace.
And the Ghuzz dwelt in their houses.
And the Caliph sent a letter to the Sultan:
"This was not my expectation,
but I had hoped that my glory would increase even more through your arrival,
and the faith would be glorified by your closeness to me.
And though I have suffered these contrary things,
my trust is in God."
And the Sultan replied:
"I am subject to your command.
And these things which happened —
you know that it was on account of these wicked Turks who were in your service
that this occurred,
and I am not to blame."
Then the Sultan commanded,
and they incited the elephants that were with him against the ten Turks who had made the brawl,
and they trampled and killed them.
And the Sultan took control over Baghdad,
and he appointed governors and tax-collectors from his own people.
And the former Turks of Baghdad —
some of them became bakers,
and some of them sellers of vegetables {OCR?},
and others stokers of baths.
And the Ghuzz dominated the country and devastated it.
And agriculture ceased;
and a plow-ox was sold for twenty zuzē,
and an ass for ten zuzē.
And they struck dirhams and dinars in the name of the Sultan.
And the Sultan increased the Caliph's allowances beyond what used to be given to him formerly,
when the Daylamites and Turkish slaves held sway,
by fifty thousand dinars and five hundred kōrs of wheat.
And he swore and said:
"Were it not for the many troops that are with me,
whom it is an obligation to maintain {OCR?},
everything that those Turks used to take, I would have restored to the Caliph."
And the Caliph's heart was pleased,
and he sought an alliance by marriage with them.
And there was given to him Arslan Khatun the Seljuk, the daughter of Chaghri Beg, brother of Sultan Tughril Beg.
And the Sultan built for himself a large mansion beside the Caliph's palace.
And the Caliph sent a gilded throne studded with precious stones,
and set it up in it.
The Sultan sat upon it,
and the nobles would enter to do him homage.
And in the year 448,
448 of the Arabs [1056-1057 AD],
there occurred sickness and a great famine in Baghdad.
Even a single pomegranate was sold for a dinar,
and medicinal drugs were not to be found.
And [the dead] multiplied
